clinicalPearls: Arises from heterozygous activating (gain-of-function) variants in MTOR, the serine/threonine kinase at the heart of the mTOR signalling pathway that governs cell growth, proliferation and metabolism
The core triad is megalencephaly or macrocephaly, intellectual disability and a recognisable facial gestalt with frontal bossing, a long face and downslanting palpebral fissures
Seizures are common and may be difficult to control, and some children show autistic features

As a disorder of mTOR-pathway overactivation it sits within the mTORopathies, sharing mechanistic ground with focal cortical dysplasia and tuberous sclerosis rather than with the chromatin-modifier syndromes
Skin findings such as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches may be present, reflecting somatic mosaicism in some individuals
Because the pathway is druggable, mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus are being explored in a research and specialist setting for selected manifestations
Diagnosis is molecular, identifying a recurrent activating MTOR variant, and mosaic cases may require testing of affected tissue or deep sequencing
reference.pathophysiology: MTOR encodes the catalytic kinase of two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, which integrate growth-factor and nutrient signals to drive protein synthesis, cell growth and proliferation while restraining autophagy. Gain-of-function variants lock the kinase in an overactive state, so downstream signalling proceeds even without normal upstream cues. In the developing brain this excessive signalling enlarges neurons and disturbs cortical organisation, producing megalencephaly, epilepsy and intellectual disability, while its effects in other tissues account for the overgrowth and pigmentary skin changes. Because the abnormality lies in a well-characterised and pharmacologically accessible pathway, rational suppression of mTOR activity is an area of active therapeutic interest.
additionalDifferentials: Megalencephaly-capillary malformation and megalencephaly-polymicrogaly spectrum (PIK3CA, AKT3, PIK3R2)
Focal cortical dysplasia type II from somatic mTOR-pathway variants
Other overgrowth syndromes with intellectual disability
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing for germline MTOR variants, with deep sequencing if mosaicism is suspected
Brain MRI to document megalencephaly and any cortical malformation
Serial head circumference and growth measurements
Neurodevelopmental and behavioural assessment including autism screening
Dermatological examination for pigmentary skin changes with tissue sampling if mosaicism is considered
Specialist review regarding the role of mTOR pathway inhibition in selected cases
redFlags: Escalating or refractory seizures requiring urgent neurological review
Rapidly increasing head circumference or signs of raised intracranial pressure
Feeding difficulties with faltering growth in infancy
reference.prognosis: The condition is lifelong, with intellectual disability that ranges from mild to severe and epilepsy that may be difficult to control in some children; overall outlook depends heavily on seizure burden and developmental trajectory, and emerging mTOR-pathway therapies may in future modify aspects of the phenotype though evidence remains preliminary.
pitfalls: Overlooking somatic mosaicism, so that standard blood testing yields a falsely negative result
Confusing the picture with tuberous sclerosis and missing the specific MTOR diagnosis
Attributing macrocephaly to a benign familial cause and delaying evaluation of developmental delay and seizures
Initiating mTOR inhibition outside a specialist framework without appropriate monitoring
references: Nature Reviews — mTOR signalling in growth and neurodevelopmental disorders
management: There is no cure; mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus are being explored in specialist and research settings for selected manifestations of this mTORopathy.
Antiepileptic drug therapy for seizures, which may be difficult to control and require combination regimens.
Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, and individualised educational support for intellectual disability.
Behavioural support including assessment and management of autistic features.
Surveillance with serial head circumference, brain MRI for megalencephaly and cortical malformation, and electroencephalography where seizures occur.
Coordinate care across paediatric neurology, clinical genetics and developmental paediatrics, with dermatology review of pigmentary skin changes.
Genetic counselling for the activating MTOR variant, noting possible mosaicism when assessing recurrence risk and family members.
